extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; urban literate public; makers of public monuments, sign-writers, composers, and social commentators
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative rules (presented wryly) about designing public monuments, epitaphs, shop-signs, and musical recitative so they suit public taste and truth of character. Includes brief behavioural rules for a mock 'amorous club.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaphs should avoid extravagant praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Some of them were covered with such extravagant Epitaphs, that, if it were possible for the dead Person to be acquainted with them, he would blush at the Praises which his Friends have bestowed upon him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: overblown panegyrics that misrepresent or flatter the deceased beyond truth. Prefer modest, honest commendation rather than hyperbolic adulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscriptions must be intelligible to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: There are others so excessively modest, that they deliver the Character of the Person departed in Greek or Hebrew, and by that Means are not understood once in a Twelve-month.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use accessible language for public memorials; avoid obscure classical languages or erudite modes that render the inscription unreadable by ordinary visitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monuments should represent the true character and services of the person
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of the brave rough English Admiral... he is represented on his Tomb by the Figure of a Beau... The Inscription... acquaints us only with the Manner of his Death, in which it was impossible for him to reap any Honour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure sculptural depiction and inscriptions reflect the individual's deeds and distinguishing character (e.g., an admiral should be shown with naval attributes, and inscriptions should celebrate accomplishments rather than only manner of death).

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit monuments and inscriptions to men of learning and genius before execution
rubrics_metrics.description: they should be submitted to the Perusal of Men of Learning and Genius before they are put in Execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solicit scholarly or tasteful review of public memorial designs and wording to avoid errors of taste, inappropriate iconography, or absurd conceits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate professional iconography on monuments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Monuments of their Admirals... represent them like themselves; and are adorned with rostral Crowns and naval Ornaments, with beautiful Festoons of [Seaweed], Shells, and Coral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match decorative elements to the deceased's profession or achievements (naval emblems for seafarers, etc.) rather than generic or irrelevant ornamentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epitaphs should record more than mere birth and death dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Most of them recorded nothing else of the buried Person, but that he was born upon one Day and died upon another: The whole History of his Life, being comprehended in those two Circumstances...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bare, sterile registers of existence. Memorial inscriptions should convey something of the person's life or character beyond mere dates to avoid appearing satirical or pointless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove monstrous and absurd public signs
rubrics_metrics.description: My first Task, therefore, should be, like that of Hercules, to clear the City from Monsters... flying Pigs, and Hogs in Armour, with many other Creatures more extraordinary than any in the desarts of Africk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ban or reform grotesque, fanciful, or ludicrous sign-figures that undermine civic taste or invite ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid joining jarring or incongruous elements in a single sign
rubrics_metrics.description: I would forbid, that Creatures of jarring and incongruous Natures should be joined together in the same Sign; such as the Bell and the Neats-tongue, the Dog and Gridiron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design signs with internal coherence; do not combine unrelated symbols just because they are available—avoid visual or conceptual mismatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shop signs should bear affinity to the wares sold
rubrics_metrics.description: I would enjoin every Shop to make use of a Sign which bears some Affinity to the Wares in which it deals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select imagery that communicates the business's trade (e.g., a cook should not have a boot sign). This aids recognition and tastefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tradesmen should display marks of their trade on signs
rubrics_metrics.description: I think it highly proper for those who actually profess the Trade, to shew some such Marks of it before their Doors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage literal or emblematic tools/marks of the trade on a sign to signal vocation; this practice is preferable to unrelated heraldic or fanciful devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use name-based devices when appropriate to identify the owner
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Name gives an Occasion for an ingenious Sign-post, I would likewise advise the Owner to take that Opportunity of letting the World know who he is... Mrs. Salmon... erected before her House the Figure of the Fish that is her Namesake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punning or nominative signs (visual plays on the proprietor's name) are acceptable—indeed recommended—when they clarify identity and provide tasteful wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate copying/quartering of another's sign or arms
rubrics_metrics.description: it is usual for a young Tradesman, at his first setting up, to add to his own Sign that of the Master whom he serv'd... This I take to have given Rise to many of those Absurdities... I would, therefore, establish certain Rules, for the determining how far one Tradesman may 'give' the Sign of another, and in what Cases he may be allowed to quarter it with his own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid indiscriminate adoption of another's sign; create clear rules about appropriation and quartering so that signage remains meaningful and not an incoherent patchwork.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs reveal the humour or temper of the inhabitant
rubrics_metrics.description: I can give a shrewd Guess at the Humour of the Inhabitant by the Sign that hangs before his Door.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose signage deliberately—while entertaining, signs function as social signals and reflect the proprietor's projected character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use Italian recitative with English words
rubrics_metrics.description: The only Fault I find in our present Practice, is the making use of Italian Recitative with English Words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid applying a musical recitative idiom built for one language directly to another without adaptation; mismatches between musical phrasing and linguistic accent lead to comic or unintelligible effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recitative and melodic cadences must match the tone/accent of the language
rubrics_metrics.description: For this Reason, the Recitative Musick in every Language, should be as different as the Tone or Accent of each Language... the Cadences in the Recitativo bear a remote Affinity to the Tone of their Voices in ordinary Conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose vocal recitative with sensitivity to the prosody and accentual patterns of the language so that musical inflections mirror natural speech and correctly express passion and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt foreign musical graces to native taste rather than supplant the native style
rubrics_metrics.description: I would allow the Italian Opera to lend our English Musick as much as may grace and soften it, but never entirely to annihilate and destroy it... Let the Infusion be as strong as you please, but still let the Subject Matter of it be English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Borrow technical refinements from other traditions (graces, modulations) but rework them to fit national language, sensibility, and subject-matter instead of wholesale imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art should conform to popular taste; fit music to the people's genius
rubrics_metrics.description: Musick, Architecture, and Painting, as well as Poetry, and Oratory, are to deduce their Laws and Rules from the general Sense and Taste of Mankind... A Composer should fit his Musick to the Genius of the People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value audience reception and native sensibilities when setting aesthetic rules—taste is the normative touchstone for public arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Music must communicate passion to ordinary ears
rubrics_metrics.description: A Man of an ordinary Ear is a Judge whether a Passion is express'd in proper Sounds, and whether the Melody of those Sounds be more or less pleasing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not compose solely for specialist or 'chromatic' ears; ensure expressive clarity so typical listeners perceive the intended emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage design and costuming should be appropriate to character and genre
rubrics_metrics.description: I remember... a couple of Rivers appear in red Stockings; and Alpheus, instead of having his Head covered with Sedge and Bull-Rushes, making Love in a fair full-bottomed Perriwig... This is what we call Folly and Impertinence;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid incongruous or anachronistic costuming and scenic detail that produce ridicule rather than verisimilitude; visual elements should serve the narrative and character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve national arts by civilizing native forms with selected foreign graces
rubrics_metrics.description: Signior Baptist Lully acted like a Man of Sense... he did not pretend to extirpate the French Musick, and plant the Italian in its stead; but only to Cultivate and Civilize it with innumerable Graces and Modulations which he borrow'd from the Italian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model for reform: enhance indigenous arts by selective, respectful incorporation of useful techniques from abroad rather than wholesale replacement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Club membership/performance rules (amorous club satire)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Mistress, and a Poem in her Praise, will introduce any Candidate: Without the latter no one can be admitted;... To speak disrespectfully of any Woman, is Expulsion... We look upon a Man as no Company, that does not sigh five times in a Quarter of an Hour; and look upon a Member as very absurd, that is so much himself as to make a direct Answer to a Question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Satirical rules governing an 'Amorous Club': admission requires composing a poem and praising a mistress; members must observe performative signs of passion (sighing, rhetorical behaviour) and refrain from disparaging women. These are prescriptive within the fictional club's norms.
